channel.title: Curio Files
channel.description: True, faintly disgusting things from history, science and art. New file Monday, Wednesday, Saturday.

item.title: Wednesday, September 23
item.description: Every good con starts with a small, believable lie, and 1920s New Jersey had a beauty. Girls barely out of school sat at long tables in the U.S. Radium Corporation, painting watch dials with glow in the dark paint made from actual radium. Their bosses taught them a trick to keep the brush tip fine, lip, dip, paint. Put the bristles in your mouth, dip in the radium paste, paint the numbers, repeat,...

item.title: Monday, September 21
item.description:
There is a particular kind of horror that comes from something familiar turning strange right in front of you. A brewery. A painting. A puddle of pond scum. A bucket of chowder. All ordinary, all hiding something you did not expect, and today they all get their moment.

item.title: Saturday, September 19
item.description:
Time is a liar, and nowhere does it lie harder than in the four scenes we're digging up today.
Start in Rome, January 897. Pope Formosus has been dead for nine months, buried, decomposing, doing what corpses do best. item.title: Wednesday, September 16
item.description: Every good disaster starts the same way, something gets bottled up until it can't be anymore. Boston, January 1919, the North End is stacked with tenements and a steel tank fifty feet tall, holding two point three million gallons of molasses meant for munitions and rum. item.title: Monday, September 14
item.description: Every good disaster starts with somebody deciding a bad idea is actually a great one. Strasbourg, July 1518, a woman named Frau Troffea steps into the street and starts dancing. Not fun dancing. Not wedding dancing. The kind of dancing where your feet bleed through your shoes and you keep going anyway. item.title: Saturday, September 12
item.description: Picture London in July of 1858, when the Thames stopped being a river and started being a punishment. Decades of raw sewage had baked in the summer heat until the smell rolled off the water like a physical wall. Members of Parliament, sitting right on the riverbank, soaked their curtains in chloride of lime and still gagged through debates. Newspapers called it the Great Stink, which undersells it...

item.description:
